series.title: AI Tips
series.summary: Short, practical lessons on working with AI assistants and agents. Each one names a common failure, explains why it happens, and leaves you with one habit to fix it.

lessons.title: Paste First, Ask Second
lessons.summary: When an AI gives you a useless answer, it is usually not the AI's fault: you described the problem instead of showing it. Without the real material, it can only guess. Paste the screenshot, document, error message, or email thread first, and the same question gets a specific, usable answer.
lessons.rule: Paste first, ask second. Hand over the screenshot, document, error message, or email thread before you type a single word of your question.

lessons.title: Ask for Proof, Not “Done”
lessons.summary: When a bot says “done”, it is usually reporting the status of the step it ran, not whether the outcome you wanted is true. Five short examples show the gap, and none of them is a bot misbehaving. The fix is to ask for something only a real result can produce.
lessons.rule: Ask for the artifact, not the status: the ticket numbers, a screenshot on the actual device, counts per item instead of a job status, a link you can click yourself. No artifact means it hasn't happened yet.

lessons.title: Define the Number Before You Ask for It
lessons.summary: Ask a bot for a number with a loose word in it and it will quietly pick a meaning, then hand you a confident, wrong answer. This tip shows how one word like "got" or "orders" can mean several populations, and the one extra sentence that removes the guess.
lessons.rule: Before asking any agent or analyst for a number, state three things: the exact metric (which event, which status), the source system your team signs off on, and the as-of date. Where you can, add a number you already know ("this should land near X, tell me if it doesn't") so the answer has to reconcile. If a vague question gets a fast, confident answer, treat that speed as the warning sign and ask what interpretation was used.

lessons.title: Know What the Bot Can Actually Reach
lessons.summary: A bot's usefulness is bounded by what it's connected to, and it almost never tells you where that boundary is. Five generic examples show how a missing link, an unread thread reply or a doc it can't write turns into something that sounds like success.
lessons.rule: Before handing a bot a task, confirm which bot you're talking to and what it's connected to. Treat any "I'll write / file / run / log it" as a claim about access, not a status, and check it can actually do that. Remember that an approval, a chat request to borrow access, or an untagged thread reply doesn't grant access or reach the bot. Access is granted where the tool is administered.

lessons.title: Don't Trust "I Can't"
lessons.summary: A bot's "I can't" is often a prediction, not a test. It hasn't tried, or it guessed at your role. This tip shows how to tell a soft refusal from a real limit, so you push on the right ones and never around a genuine guardrail.
lessons.rule: When an agent says it can't, check whether it names the missing piece. A bare refusal: ask it to find another permitted route and try before saying no. A named blocker (a key, an account link, someone's approval): ask it to confirm it actually checked, and if it holds, go get that piece rather than arguing. Ask for the goal, not the method, state your role and access up front, pre-authorise a second attempt, and ask for the exact step that stopped it. "Find a way" never means working around a real limit.

lessons.title: Teach It Once
lessons.summary: Knowledge is what a bot has picked up. Skills are jobs you've written down for it. This tip shows how to save what a bot works out so nobody repeats it, why a good skill is mostly guardrails, and how saved rules can fence a credential that does more than the job needs.
lessons.rule: When you explain the same thing to a bot a second time, or it finally gets something right after getting it wrong, have it save the rule. Write skills mostly as boundaries: when to act, when not to, whose data, where to report, what to do when unsure, and when to stop. Where a credential can do more than the job needs, add an explicit rule (e.g. reads only, no writes without approval), but treat it as a seatbelt, not a vault, and use a narrower credential for anything that genuinely matters.

lessons.title: The Second Message
lessons.summary: Most people read the first answer and stop. Either they settle for it or give up on the tool. One follow-up line in the same chat usually turns a generic draft into a usable one, and asking the A.I. to interview you first is better still.
lessons.rule: Treat the first answer as a draft, not a verdict. Reply in the same conversation with one of three follow-ups: say specifically what's wrong, ask for a different shape, or give it something concrete to work from. For anything you'll care about, start by telling it: "Before you write it, ask me what you need to know." Don't open a new chat to fix a draft, because that throws away the context it has built.

lessons.title: Stop Re-Explaining Yourself
lessons.summary: If every Claude chat starts with you re-explaining your job and re-attaching the same file, a Project fixes it: shared knowledge and instructions in one place. This tip covers what sharing a project hands over (and what stays private), the permission choices, and where Cowork tasks run.
lessons.rule: When you find yourself re-uploading the same files or repeating the same instructions, put them in a Claude Project: files in project knowledge, standing rules in project instructions. Share the project with the people who'd benefit. Sharing hands over knowledge and instructions, while each person's chats stay private unless they share one deliberately. Choose org-wide or invite-only, and can-view or can-edit. If a task "can't see" your local folder, check whether it needs the desktop app open.

lessons.title: Claude Code Isn't Just for Developers
lessons.summary: Claude Code's name keeps most non-developers away, but it works on any folder of ordinary files, driven by plain-English requests. This tip shows what it can do with screenshots, invoices and transcripts, what "it's a terminal" really means, and how to start in five minutes.
lessons.rule: For any job that means reading, renaming, or pulling information across many files in one folder, try Claude Code before doing it by hand: install it, point it at the folder, and describe the outcome in plain English. Use Esc to interrupt, /help to see what it can do, and the desktop app if you'd rather not use a terminal. Check the result before relying on it.

lessons.title: The Label Is Not the Definition
lessons.summary: The most common mistake in six weeks of bots' self-written lessons: trusting what a field is called instead of what it counts. A number with the wrong definition still ties out and reconciles, so nothing looks wrong and it travels.
lessons.rule: Before using or explaining a number, find out what it actually counts. Read the definition, not the field name. Treat a surprising number as a likely definition problem before treating it as a story. When the source is unclear, ask the data owner which table holds the number they actually sign off on, and say which dataset every reported number came from.

lessons.title: Your Bot in the Meeting
lessons.summary: A notetaker records one call and summarises it. A bot that's connected to your team's work can answer questions live, turn action items into real tickets, and remember what was decided last week. This tip shows how to try it on one meeting, and the limit that catches people out.
lessons.rule: Try a connected team bot on one recurring meeting, the one where someone always says "I'll check and get back to you." Invite it (or give it the link) and admit it from the waiting room. Afterwards, if you invited it, share the notes yourself, because often only the inviter receives them. Expect a first version: it may not see screen shares or speak aloud yet.

lessons.title: Brief the Next Chat
lessons.summary: Long chats drift without warning: early decisions count for less and can fall out of view. When a chat gets long, have it write a handoff and carry on in a fresh chat.
lessons.rule: When a chat gets long, brief the next one: the goal and the limits, every decision so far, what's still open, and read it before you paste it.

lessons.title: Open the Source
lessons.summary: AI-supplied citations can be perfectly formatted and completely invented, and pushed on a dead link a model may insist the page changed. A reference you haven't opened is a claim, not a source.
lessons.rule: Open it before you use it: click the link, check the title and authors, find the sentence you need on the page. Nothing to open? Not a source yet.

lessons.title: Ask It to Disagree
lessons.summary: Models lean toward the view already in your question, so a yes to a leading question isn't a second opinion. Ask for the case against before you ask for advice: a review, not a fight.
lessons.rule: Ask for the case against: leave your answer out of the question, ask for the strongest case against and how you could be wrong, then ask what it recommends.

lessons.title: Treat Memory Like Notes
lessons.summary: AI memory is a small set of saved notes, not a mind. Notes can be never saved, saved wrong, off-topic or stale, and they won't keep up unless you update them.
lessons.rule: Treat memory like notes: say what matters in the prompt, don't assume a new chat knows, read your memory now and then, and fix or delete what's wrong.

lessons.title: Don't Fire and Forget
lessons.summary: Agents act on real systems, and a rule typed into a prompt is not a lock. Put the lock in access and approval settings, and keep the judgment for steps you can't undo.
lessons.rule: Set the stop before you start: say what done looks like, limit what it can touch, require approval before delete, reset, push or send, and watch the first few steps.

series.title: Software Engineering 101
series.summary: Ten short lessons on building software when AI agents do much of the building. Each lesson ends with one rule, written so your agents can follow it too.

lessons.title: Plan, Build, Verify (and When to Skip It)
lessons.summary: How do you fix code you don't understand when you only get one shot? Split the work into four roles: a person who owns the problem, a planner, a builder, and a verifier on a different model that can only read and report. Loop until the verifier runs out of serious things to say. Then: what that costs, and when a lighter path is good enough.
lessons.rule: If a change can't be rolled back, and the person asking can't check it themselves, it gets an independent review, on a different model, before it ships. That's the floor. The longer list, of when to use the full pattern, is judgment.

lessons.title: Rigor Follows Risk
lessons.summary: A patch in ten minutes or the root cause in two days? Redeploy speed is only half the question: a redeploy fixes the code, but it doesn't undo what the code did. Product shape is uncertain and easy to change, so ship it rough behind a flag. Correctness you can't undo, meaning money, customer data, and messages, gets the root cause.
lessons.rule: Rough is fine for product shape. It is never fine for money, customer data, or anything that can't be undone. If a piece of work is both, the stricter standard wins. For that kind of work: stop any live damage first, then find the root cause, and give the estimate in usage, not in days.

lessons.title: Principles Over Languages
lessons.summary: Why a computer science education built on ideas, not languages, still pays off, and why it matters more now that agents write the syntax.
lessons.rule: When you make a design choice, explain the principle behind it, in plain words. Not just the framework feature you used.

lessons.title: The Abstraction Ladder
lessons.summary: AI coding is one more rung on a ladder that runs from logic gates up. Stay at the top, and know when to send your agent down a rung.
lessons.rule: Break a task into small pieces that each do one thing. And when something on one layer doesn't add up, look at the layer below, before you change anything.

lessons.title: Understand Before You Change
lessons.summary: A perfect fix for the wrong problem is still wrong. Own the problem, restate it, reproduce and trace it, then fix the cause.
lessons.rule: Before planning, restate the problem in plain words, and confirm it with the person who gave you the task. They own the problem. Before fixing, reproduce it if you can, and trace what actually happens. Then fix the cause, not the symptom.

lessons.title: Say What, Not How
lessons.summary: Like a database optimizer, an agent does its best work when you state the outcome and the limits, not the steps. Too tight and too loose both cost you.
lessons.rule: A spec states the outcome, and what must not break. It doesn't dictate steps, unless a step is itself a requirement. And before you start the work, give a cost forecast.

lessons.title: Old Patterns, New Clothes
lessons.summary: Pair programming, test-first and code review still work with agents in the seats. Cheaper tests change the trade, and three anti-patterns to watch for.
lessons.rule: Write the failing test before the fix. No bug fix merges without a test that would have caught the bug. And the agent that wrote the code never approves it.

lessons.title: Agile at Agent Speed
lessons.summary: Keep every scrum ceremony, but run the loop daily. Deploy continuously, ship features switched off behind a flag, and write down what you learned.
lessons.rule: Ship small changes continuously, once the automated checks pass. New features ship switched off, behind a flag. A person decides when each one turns on, for one client or a small group first. And end every session with a short written note on what was learned.

lessons.title: Know What It Costs
lessons.summary: AI usage is the new currency of software. See the spend, the limit and a priced forecast before you start, and remember that owning software costs more than building it.
lessons.rule: Before any sizable task, show the spend so far, the limit, and a forecast for each path. If you can't see a number, say so, and label an estimate as an estimate. Afterward, record what it actually cost. And before you build something new, check what already exists.

lessons.title: Strict About Data, Relaxed About the Perimeter
lessons.summary: Be uncompromising about customer personal data and card data, pragmatic about where internal apps live, and see the whole series on one screen.
lessons.rule: Never store, log, or send raw card data. Customer personal data stays out of logs, errors, test data, and your own working notes. Internal apps sit behind company sign-in, on every route. And any change that touches personal data or payments gets an independent review.

series.title: Software Engineering 201
series.summary: 101 was about one piece of work: getting one fix or one feature right. That's the loop. 201 is the layer above: how work is split, what runs in parallel, where a person decides, and how each run makes the next one better. That's the graph.

lessons.title: From Loop to Graph
lessons.summary: A loop makes one piece of work correct. A graph decides which pieces exist and which can run at the same time. Built around how three Software Engineering 101 lessons were made side by side, each with its own review.
lessons.rule: Before any job with more than one part, write down the pieces, and which can run at the same time. Then run each piece as its own loop, checked on its own.

lessons.title: Find the Real Dependencies
lessons.summary: “And then” is not a dependency. If nothing crosses between two steps, they don't need to wait for each other.
